title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night seven: a dark, fearsome form of the goddess arrives on the night Saraswati's nights begin, and in some homes the books go to rest

segments.voice: Yesterday was night six of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Katyayani, and Uma coming home to a mother waiting at the door. Who did you ask after? Day one thousand one hundred fifteen.

A schoolbook, a pen, a harmonium, a child's slate. In some homes, around this point in Navaratri, they're stacked together in front of an image of Saraswati, the goddess of learning, music and speech, and decorated with a little sandal paste and a flower. And then nobody touches them. No homework from those books, no practice on that instrument, until the festival is over. In the three-by-three way of keeping the festival, Saraswati's nights begin about now. But the seventh name in the Kavacha's list is not gentle at all.
screen: `BOOKS STACKED BEFORE SARASWATI.` → `NOBODY TOUCHES THEM.` → `THE SEVENTH NAME IS NOT GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Her name is Kalaratri. You can hear the word ratri in it, night, the same word that's in Navaratri. In paintings of this night she's black as a moonless sky, hair loose and wild, breath like fire, sometimes riding a donkey. Nothing about her is there to reassure you. And yet devotees who keep the nine forms give her a second name, Shubhankari, the one who does good. The fearsome form is the protecting one. So here's the odd thing about the curriculum's order. On the very night the learning nights begin, the goddess comes as night itself. Why put them together? One way to read it: real learning starts where you're scared. The thing you avoid looking at, the subject you're sure you're bad at, the conversation you keep putting off. Kalaratri is the form that walks straight into the dark, and Saraswati is the clarity on the other side. Then the books. Setting them down before Saraswati says something simple: knowledge isn't only a tool you pick up and use. It's a gift you can bow to. For a few days the pens and books and instruments rest, the way a field rests, and the people who use them rest too. When the festival is over, they're picked up again with a blessing, and in some places little children write their first letters that day. So night seven teaches a pair. Face the dark, and then honor what helps you see. Put down what you know for a few days, so you can pick it up again as a gift.
screen: `KALARATRI: NIGHT IN HER NAME.` · `FEARSOME, AND SHE DOES GOOD.` · `LEARNING STARTS WHERE YOU'RE SCARED.` · `BOOKS AT REST, PICKED UP AS A GIFT.` · then, large: `FACE THE DARK. HONOR WHAT HELPS YOU SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: into the dark, then toward the light. Settle, close your eyes, and let the breath slow. Let the dark behind your eyelids be just what it is. Then turn toward one thing you've been afraid to learn or to look at: a subject, a skill, a conversation. Don't solve it. Just stop looking away from it for the length of a few breaths. Then let one small first step toward it come to mind, a question you could ask, a page you could read. If you pray, you can ask Saraswati, or God, for clarity, in words you already know. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night seven: Kalaratri, the dark, fearsome form, on the night Saraswati's nights begin.
Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Today, take the first small step toward the thing you've been afraid to learn: one question, out loud. Day one thousand one hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: In some Hindu homes, especially in South India, books, pens and instruments are placed before Saraswati in the last days of Navaratri and not used until Vijayadashami; where the nine forms are kept, the seventh night honors Kalaratri.

notes: Night seven on this writer's count (1109 = night one).
Kalaratri's iconography (dark, loose hair, fiery breath, donkey) and her other name Shubhankari come from Navadurga lore, not the Kavacha; confirm.

Placing books and instruments before Saraswati (often from the Moola nakshatra day) until Vijayadashami, and children writing first letters that day (vidyarambham, especially in Kerala): described with 'in some homes' / 'in some places'. Confirm timing phrasing 'around this point'.
